definition: Price-to-Earnings Ratio — the ratio of a company's share price to its earnings per share. A higher P/E can indicate higher growth expectations; a lower P/E may indicate lower expectations or possible undervaluation.
Market Capitalisation — the total market value of a company's outstanding shares, calculated as share price × total shares outstanding.
The S&P BSE SENSEX is a benchmark index of 30 major companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE).
A major Indian stock market index representing 50 large companies listed on the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
A financial ratio showing how much a company pays in dividends each year relative to its stock price. Annual Dividends ÷ Stock Price × 100.
A market condition characterised by rising prices and generally positive investor sentiment. A common technical definition is a 20% or greater rise from a recent low.
A market condition characterised by falling prices and widespread pessimism. A common technical definition is a 20% or greater decline from a recent high.
Foreign Institutional Investor — an investor or institution from outside India that invests in Indian financial markets.
Domestic Institutional Investor — Indian institutions such as mutual funds, insurance companies and banks that invest in Indian markets.
A measure of how much and how quickly the price of an investment moves. Higher volatility generally means larger price swings.
The highest price at which a security has traded during the previous 52 weeks.
A technical indicator that calculates the average price over a specific period, such as 50 days or 200 days.
Earnings Per Share — the portion of a company's profit attributable to each outstanding share. EPS = Net Income ÷ Shares Outstanding.
The rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends money to commercial banks. It is an important monetary-policy tool.
A mutual fund or ETF designed to track a particular market index instead of actively trying to outperform it.
A financial security representing ownership in a company. Owning stock can give an investor a claim on part of the company's assets and profits.
A single unit of ownership in a company.
Ownership value in a company. For an investor, equity usually means ownership through shares.
A type of company ownership that usually provides voting rights and a claim on profits after other obligations are paid.
A type of company ownership that generally receives dividends before common shareholders and may have preferential claims on company assets.
A company with a relatively large market capitalisation compared with other companies in its market.
A company with a medium-sized market capitalisation compared with other companies in its market.
A company with a relatively small market capitalisation compared with larger companies.
A well-established company that is generally considered financially strong and relatively mature.
A stock of a company expected to grow its revenue or profits faster than the broader market.
A stock that appears relatively inexpensive compared with measures such as earnings, assets or cash flow.
A stock belonging to a business whose demand tends to remain relatively stable even during economic downturns.
A stock whose business performance tends to move closely with economic conditions.
A very low-priced stock, often associated with smaller companies and potentially higher volatility and liquidity risk.
An index designed to track relatively large, established and financially significant companies.
Initial Public Offering — when a private company offers its shares to the public for the first time and becomes publicly listed.
Follow-on Public Offer — a public offering of shares by a company that is already listed.
The market where new securities are issued and sold to investors.
The market where investors buy and sell securities that have already been issued.
The process of a company's securities becoming available for trading on a stock exchange.
A process used in many public offerings where investor bids help determine the final issue price.
The price at which newly issued shares or securities are offered to investors.
The price at which a newly listed security begins trading on an exchange.
An offer by a company to existing shareholders to purchase additional shares under specified terms.
When a company gives existing shareholders additional shares without charging them separately, according to a specified ratio.
A corporate action that increases the number of shares while proportionally reducing the price per share, without changing the overall value of an investor's holding at the time of the split.
A corporate action that reduces the number of shares while proportionally increasing the price per share.
When a company purchases its own shares from shareholders.
A payment made by a company to its shareholders, usually from profits or accumulated reserves.
A dividend declared and paid before a company's final annual results are completed.
A dividend declared after the financial year and usually approved according to the company's applicable corporate process.
The date used to determine which shareholders are eligible to receive a corporate benefit such as a dividend or bonus.
The date from which a stock trades without the entitlement to the upcoming dividend.
Employee Stock Option Plan — a scheme that gives employees the right to acquire company shares under specified conditions.
The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before subtracting expenses.
The amount of money a company earns from selling products or services.
Revenue minus the direct costs of producing the goods or services sold.
Gross profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
Profit generated from normal business operations after operating expenses are deducted.
Operating profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
Earnings Before Interest and Taxes — profit before interest expenses and income taxes are deducted.
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization — a measure often used to compare operating performance before certain expenses.
EBITDA expressed as a percentage of revenue.
The profit remaining after a company subtracts its expenses, interest, taxes and other applicable costs from revenue.
Net profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
Profit After Tax — the profit remaining after income taxes have been accounted for.
Profit Before Tax — profit calculated before income tax is deducted.
Regular costs required to run a business, such as salaries, rent, administration and marketing.
Capital Expenditure — money a company spends on long-term assets such as buildings, machinery, technology or equipment.
Operating Expenditure — regular costs required to operate a business.
Cash generated by a company after accounting for the capital spending needed to maintain or grow the business.
Cash generated or used by a company's normal business operations.
The movement of money into and out of a company, investment or individual's finances.
Current assets minus current liabilities. It helps show a company's short-term financial position.
Return on Equity — a measure of how efficiently a company generates profit from shareholders' equity.
Return on Assets — a measure of how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.
Return on Invested Capital — a measure of how efficiently a company generates profit from the capital invested in its business.
A ratio comparing a company's debt with shareholders' equity.
A measure of how easily a company can pay interest on its debt using its operating earnings.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. It is commonly used to assess short-term financial strength.
A liquidity ratio that compares assets that can be converted into cash relatively quickly with current liabilities.
A ratio showing how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate revenue.
A measure of how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory during a period.
A financial statement showing a company's assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a specific point in time.
A financial statement showing a company's revenue, expenses and profit or loss over a period.
A financial statement showing how cash moved through a company during a period.
Things a company or person owns that have economic value.
Money or obligations that a company or person owes to others.
The residual value belonging to shareholders after subtracting liabilities from assets.
Assets expected to be converted into cash or used within a relatively short period, generally within one year.
Financial obligations generally due within one year.
Profit a company keeps in the business instead of distributing it entirely to shareholders.
The accounting process of spreading the cost of a physical asset over its useful life.
The process of gradually spreading the cost of certain intangible assets or financial obligations over time.
An accounting asset that can arise when a company acquires another company for more than the fair value of its identifiable net assets.
A non-physical asset such as patents, trademarks, copyrights or certain intellectual property.
A physical asset such as buildings, machinery, vehicles or equipment.
An accounting method where income and expenses are recorded when they are earned or incurred rather than only when cash changes hands.
Money customers owe a company for goods or services already provided.
Money a company owes suppliers or other parties for goods or services already received.
Goods and materials a company holds for sale or for use in producing products.
A reduction in the recorded value of an asset when its value is believed to have fallen significantly.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — accounting rules and standards used to prepare financial statements in certain jurisdictions.
International Financial Reporting Standards — accounting standards used in many countries for preparing financial statements.
Price-to-Book Ratio — a company's market price compared with its book value per share.
Price-to-Sales Ratio — a company's market value or share price compared with its sales.
Price/Earnings-to-Growth Ratio — a valuation measure that compares a company's P/E ratio with its expected earnings growth rate.
A measure of a company's overall business value that considers its market value, debt and cash.
Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA Ratio — a valuation measure comparing a company's enterprise value with EBITDA.
Enterprise Value-to-Sales Ratio — a valuation measure comparing enterprise value with revenue.
A valuation ratio comparing a company's market value with the cash generated by its operations.
Free cash flow compared with a company's market value, showing cash generation relative to the company's price.
An estimate of what an investment may be worth based on its underlying financial characteristics rather than its current market price.
An estimated reasonable value for an asset based on relevant information and valuation methods.
The difference between an investment's estimated intrinsic value and its market price, providing some protection against valuation mistakes.
Discounted Cash Flow — a valuation method that estimates an investment's value by calculating the present value of expected future cash flows.
A valuation method where different parts of a company are valued separately and then added together.
Relative Strength Index — a technical indicator that measures the strength and speed of recent price movements, usually on a scale from 0 to 100.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence — a technical indicator that compares moving averages to help identify changes in momentum and trends.
A technical indicator consisting of a moving average and bands around it that help show price volatility.
Volume Weighted Average Price — the average traded price of a security during a period, weighted by trading volume.
A price area where buying interest may be strong enough to slow or stop a decline.
A price area where selling interest may be strong enough to slow or stop a rise.
A price movement through an important support or resistance level that traders may interpret as a potential change in trend.
The general direction in which the price of a security or market is moving.
A market movement characterised by generally rising prices and higher highs and higher lows.
A market movement characterised by generally falling prices and lower highs and lower lows.
The number of shares or contracts traded during a specific period.
A measure of how broadly stocks are participating in a market movement, such as how many stocks are rising versus falling.
The strength or speed of an asset's recent price movement.
An order to buy or sell a security immediately at the best available market price.
An order to buy or sell a security only at a specified price or better.
An order designed to limit a potential loss by triggering an order when a specified price is reached.
A stop-loss that automatically moves with the price when the investment moves in a favourable direction.
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security.
The lowest price at which a seller is currently willing to sell a security.
The difference between the highest available buying price and the lowest available selling price.
A list of current buy and sell orders waiting to be matched in a market.
A view of the buy and sell orders available at different prices for a security.
Buying and selling a security within the same trading day rather than holding it overnight.
A trading approach that attempts to profit from price movements over several days or weeks.
A trading approach where investments are held for weeks, months or longer based on expected larger price movements.
A trading strategy that seeks to profit when the price of a security falls, subject to applicable market rules.
A position where an investor owns an asset or has exposure expecting its value to rise.
A position designed to benefit from a decline in the value of an asset.
Using borrowed money or financial instruments to increase the size of an investment relative to the investor's own capital.
Money or collateral required to support certain leveraged trades or positions.
The number of shares that are actually taken into or delivered from investor holdings rather than simply traded and closed within the market.
A financial instrument whose value is derived from an underlying asset, security, index, interest rate or other reference.
Standardised contracts to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price on a future date.
Contracts giving the buyer the right, but generally not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price before or at expiry.
An option giving the buyer the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price under the contract terms.
An option giving the buyer the right to sell the underlying asset at the strike price under the contract terms.
The price at which an option allows the holder to buy or sell the underlying asset.
The date on which a derivative contract expires.
The price paid by an option buyer to purchase an option contract.
The total number of outstanding derivative contracts that have not yet been closed or settled.
The level of future price movement implied by the market price of an option.
A measure of how much an asset's price has actually moved in the past.
An option is in-the-money when exercising it would currently have positive intrinsic value.
An option is at-the-money when its strike price is approximately equal to the current price of the underlying asset.
An option is out-of-the-money when exercising it would currently have no positive intrinsic value.
The value an option would have if it were exercised immediately.
The part of an option's price above its intrinsic value, reflecting factors such as time remaining and expected volatility.
The tendency of an option to lose time-related value as its expiry date approaches.
An option Greek that estimates how much an option's price may change when the underlying asset moves by one unit.
An option Greek that measures how quickly an option's delta changes when the underlying price changes.
An option Greek that measures how much an option's value may decrease as time passes, all else being equal.
An option Greek that measures how sensitive an option's price is to changes in implied volatility.
An option Greek that measures how sensitive an option's price is to changes in interest rates.
Moving a futures position from an expiring contract into a later-expiry contract.
The difference between the spot price of an asset and the price of its related futures contract.
A market condition where futures prices are below the current spot price or expected future spot price.
A market condition where futures prices are higher than the current spot price.
A debt investment where an investor lends money to a government, company or other issuer in exchange for interest and repayment according to the bond's terms.
A person or institution that owns a bond and has a claim according to the bond's terms.
The government, company or other entity that issues a financial security.
The stated value of a bond or other financial instrument, often representing the amount repaid at maturity.
The nominal value assigned to a bond or security.
The interest payment a bond pays according to its stated terms.
The stated annual interest rate paid on a bond's face value.
The income or return an investment generates relative to its price or value.
The approximate annual return an investor would earn if a bond were held until maturity and payments were made as promised.
The approximate return an investor would receive if a callable bond is repaid by the issuer on its call date.
The date on which a bond or debt instrument reaches the end of its term and the principal is generally due.
A measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to changes in interest rates and how long it takes to receive its cash flows.
A measure used to estimate how much a bond's price may change when interest rates change.
A measure of how the relationship between a bond's price and interest rates changes as rates move.
An assessment of an issuer's ability to meet its debt obligations.
The difference in yield between a bond with credit risk and a comparable lower-risk bond.
Failure by a borrower or issuer to make required payments or meet specified obligations.
A bond issued by a national government.
A bond issued by a company to borrow money from investors.
A debt security issued by a government to borrow money.
A bond issued by a local or municipal government or related authority.
A debt instrument issued by a company. Depending on its structure, it may be secured or unsecured.
A bond that allows the issuer to repay the bond before its scheduled maturity under specified conditions.
A bond that does not make regular interest payments and is typically issued at a discount to its face value.
A bond whose stated interest rate remains fixed according to its terms.
A bond whose interest rate changes periodically according to a specified benchmark or formula.
A bond receiving a relatively strong credit rating and generally considered to have lower default risk than lower-rated bonds.
A bond with a relatively low credit rating and generally higher default risk, often offering higher potential yields.
A short-term debt instrument issued by companies to raise money for short-term funding needs.
A short-term money-market instrument issued by eligible financial institutions.
The part of the financial system where short-term borrowing and lending takes place.
An investment vehicle that pools money from many investors and invests it in a portfolio of securities.
Exchange-Traded Fund — a fund that trades on a stock exchange and typically holds a basket of investments.
Assets Under Management — the total value of investments managed by a fund or investment manager.
Net Asset Value — the value of a fund's assets minus its liabilities, usually expressed per unit for mutual funds.
The percentage of a fund's assets used each year to cover management and operating expenses.
Total Expense Ratio — the percentage of a fund's assets used to cover its operating expenses.
The difference between the performance of an index fund or ETF and the index it is designed to track.
A fee that may be charged when an investor withdraws money from certain mutual fund schemes within a specified period.
A mutual fund plan purchased directly from the fund house without a distributor.
A mutual fund plan purchased through a distributor or intermediary.
A fund where a manager actively selects investments according to a strategy.
A fund designed mainly to follow an index or predefined investment strategy.
Systematic Investment Plan — a method of investing a fixed amount into a mutual fund at regular intervals.
Systematic Withdrawal Plan — a facility allowing an investor to withdraw a specified amount from a mutual fund at regular intervals.
Systematic Transfer Plan — a facility allowing money to be transferred between mutual fund schemes at regular intervals, subject to scheme rules.
A professional responsible for making investment decisions for a fund.
A standardized tool used in India to show the level of risk associated with a mutual fund scheme.
A fund designed to track the performance of a particular market index.
How an investor divides money among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, cash, gold and real estate.
Spreading investments across different assets, companies or sectors to reduce concentration risk.
Adjusting a portfolio back toward its intended asset allocation after market movements change the original percentages.
The collection of investments owned by an individual or institution.
The length of time an investor expects to keep money invested before needing it.
How much investment loss or uncertainty an investor is financially and emotionally willing to accept.
An investor's financial ability to withstand losses without seriously affecting their financial goals.
The process of earning returns on both the original investment and previously earned returns.
Compound Annual Growth Rate — the average annual rate at which an investment grows over a period, assuming compounding.
The total percentage gain or loss on an investment without adjusting it to an annual rate.
A return expressed as an equivalent yearly rate.
Extended Internal Rate of Return — a method of calculating an annualized return when investments or withdrawals happen on different dates.
A risk-adjusted performance measure comparing excess return with the amount of risk taken.
A risk-adjusted return measure that focuses on harmful downside volatility.
The largest percentage decline from a portfolio's highest value to a later lowest value during a period.
Risk caused by broad market or economic factors that affects many investments.
Risk specific to a particular company or industry that can often be reduced through diversification.
The risk that changes in interest rates will negatively affect an investment, especially bonds.
The risk that changes in exchange rates will affect the value or return of an investment.
The risk that an investment cannot be bought or sold quickly at a reasonable price.
The risk of losing a large amount because too much of a portfolio is invested in one asset, company, sector or region.
The risk that a borrower or issuer will fail to meet its financial obligations.
A sustained increase in the general level of prices, reducing the purchasing power of money.
Consumer Price Index — an index measuring changes in the prices consumers pay for a basket of goods and services.
Wholesale Price Index — an index measuring changes in prices at the wholesale level.
Gross Domestic Product — the total value of goods and services produced within an economy during a specific period.
GDP adjusted for inflation so that changes in actual economic output can be measured more clearly.
GDP measured using current prices without adjusting for inflation.
The percentage change in a country's GDP over a period.
GDP divided by the population, giving an approximate measure of economic output per person.
A significant slowdown in economic activity that affects areas such as production, employment and spending.
The recurring pattern of expansion, peak, slowdown and recovery in an economy.
A period when economic activity, production, income and employment are generally increasing.
The percentage of people in the labour force who are unemployed and actively looking for work.
Purchasing Managers' Index — a survey-based indicator that provides an early signal about business activity and whether it is expanding or contracting.
A measure of how optimistic consumers feel about their income, employment and the economy.
Government decisions about taxation, spending and borrowing that influence the economy.
Central-bank actions involving interest rates and money supply intended to influence inflation, growth and economic activity.
The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks against eligible securities.
A rate associated with banks placing funds with the central bank under applicable monetary-policy operations.
Cash Reserve Ratio — the percentage of certain bank deposits that banks are required to maintain as cash reserves with the RBI.
Statutory Liquidity Ratio — the percentage of certain liabilities that banks must maintain in specified liquid assets under applicable rules.
Actions that increase the availability of money or funds in the financial system.
Actions that reduce the amount of readily available money or liquidity in the financial system.
A central-bank policy involving large-scale purchases of financial assets intended to influence financial conditions and liquidity.
A central-bank policy of reducing its balance sheet or allowing previously purchased assets to mature, which can reduce liquidity.
A situation where economic growth is weak while inflation remains high.
A sustained decline in the general level of prices across an economy.
A slowdown in the rate at which prices are rising. Prices may still increase, but more slowly.
An interest rate adjusted for inflation.
A unit equal to 0.01 percentage point. For example, 100 basis points equals 1 percentage point.
A graph showing interest rates or yields for bonds with different maturities.
A yield curve where shorter-term interest rates are higher than longer-term rates.
The extra return investors may demand for holding a longer-term bond instead of shorter-term bonds.
Foreign Institutional Investor — a foreign institution investing in Indian markets.
Domestic Institutional Investor — an Indian institution investing in financial markets.
Securities and Exchange Board of India — the regulator responsible for overseeing India's securities market and protecting investors.
Reserve Bank of India — India's central bank, responsible for monetary policy and important banking and financial-system functions.
National Stock Exchange of India — one of India's major stock exchanges.
BSE Limited — one of India's major stock exchanges.
National Securities Depository Limited — one of India's major securities depositories that holds securities electronically.
Central Depository Services (India) Limited — one of India's major securities depositories.
Depository Participant — an intermediary through which investors access depository services for holding securities electronically.
Registrar and Transfer Agent — an entity handling administrative and record-keeping services for investors and securities issuers.
Know Your Customer — the process financial institutions use to verify a customer's identity and required information.
Unique Client Code — a unique identification code used by a broker to identify a client in securities-market transactions.
Application Supported by Blocked Amount — a system used for certain Indian public issues where application money is blocked in the investor's bank account until required.
SEBI Complaints Redress System — an online platform for investors to lodge and track complaints related to the securities market.
Portfolio Management Services — a service where a professional manages an investment portfolio for a client according to an agreed strategy.
A professional or entity that provides investment advice under the applicable regulatory framework.
A professional who researches investments and may publish analysis or recommendations about securities.
A person or group that has significant control or influence over a company and is identified as a promoter under applicable rules.
The percentage of a company's shares held by its promoters.
When promoters use their shares as collateral to borrow money.
Shares used as security or collateral for a loan or other financial obligation.
Market capitalisation calculated using shares that are freely available for public trading.
A mechanism that temporarily restricts trading or price movements when specified market or security price limits are reached.
Real Estate Investment Trust — a structure that owns or finances income-producing real estate and allows investors to participate through securities.
Infrastructure Investment Trust — an investment structure that allows investors to participate in income-generating infrastructure assets.
A basic physical good that can be traded, such as gold, crude oil, natural gas or agricultural products.
The current market price at which an asset can be bought or sold for immediate delivery.
A naturally occurring liquid fossil fuel and one of the world's major traded commodities.
A precious metal widely used as an investment, store of value, jewellery material and industrial commodity.
Foreign Exchange — the global market where currencies are bought and sold.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency.
An increase in the value of one currency relative to another currency.
A decrease in the value of one currency relative to another currency.
Investment made into early-stage or high-growth companies in exchange for an ownership stake.
Investment in companies that are generally not publicly traded, often with the goal of improving and eventually selling the investment.
An individual who invests their own money in an early-stage company, often in exchange for equity.
A privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more.
Multiple on Invested Capital — how many times an investment's value or proceeds represent the original amount invested.
Distributions to Paid-In — a private-market performance measure showing how much money has been returned to investors compared with the capital they contributed.
Total Value to Paid-In — a private-market measure comparing total distributions and remaining investment value with the amount invested.
The value of everything a person owns minus everything they owe.
Money kept aside to cover unexpected expenses or loss of income without needing to sell investments or borrow heavily.
Equated Monthly Instalment — a periodic payment used to repay a loan, generally containing both principal and interest.
A numerical measure based on credit history that helps lenders assess a person's creditworthiness.
The percentage charged for borrowing money or earned for lending or saving money.
Interest calculated only on the original principal amount.
Interest calculated on the original principal plus previously accumulated interest.
The original amount of money borrowed before interest and other charges.
Money borrowed from another person or institution that must generally be repaid according to agreed terms.
A situation where a person has enough assets or income to cover living expenses without depending entirely on employment income.
Selling investments at a loss to potentially offset eligible capital gains for tax purposes, subject to applicable tax rules.
The profit made when an investment is sold for more than its purchase price.
The loss incurred when an investment is sold for less than its purchase price.
Long-Term Capital Gains — gains from selling an investment after holding it for a period that qualifies as long-term under applicable tax rules.
Short-Term Capital Gains — gains from selling an investment after holding it for a period that qualifies as short-term under applicable tax rules.
A 12-month period used by an organisation or government for accounting and financial reporting.
A 12-month period used for accounting, budgeting and financial reporting, which may differ from the calendar year.
A three-month period used by companies to report financial results.
Quarter-over-Quarter — comparing a company's results with the previous quarter.
Year-over-Year — comparing a company's results with the same period in the previous year.
Month-over-Month — comparing a metric with the previous month.
Trailing Twelve Months — a company's financial results from the most recent twelve-month period.
Management's expectations or forecasts about future company performance.
A discussion where company management explains recent financial results and answers questions from analysts or investors.
A yearly report containing important information about a company's financial performance, operations and business.
The difference between a company's reported earnings and the earnings analysts or markets were expecting.
Actions taken by a central bank to raise benchmark interest rates or reduce money supply to cool down economic growth and control inflation.
